Generalization guarantees using Vγ dimension replace training error with margin violations, counting examples not separable with margin at least γ. Additionally, ensemble classifiers can be represented as convex combinations of simpler base classifiers: hm(x) = Σ_{j=1}^m α_j h(x; θ_j).

Vγ dimension for linear classifiers ≤ R²/γ²
Ensemble classifiers as convex combinations of base classifiers

title: Ensembles of Decision Stumps and Their Complexity
summary: This concept explains ensembles composed of decision stumps, distinguishing them from decision trees, and discusses their complexity and generalization properties, including the ability to shatter any n points with 2n stumps in one dimension.
content: Ensembles considered here are formed by combining decision stumps with non-negative coefficients \( \alpha_j \) that sum to one (normalization can be done after boosting). Unlike decision trees, which recursively partition the input space into regions with uniform labels, these ensembles apply each stump over the entire input space, meaning each stump contributes to the classification of all examples. The complexity and generalization guarantees of such ensembles depend on the voting margin achieved, for example, through boosting algorithms, though the generation method is not discussed here. Importantly, ensembles of decision stumps are powerful: it is possible to shatter any set of n points in one dimension using 2n stumps. This is demonstrated by constructing pairs of stumps to reproduce the label of each point individually without affecting others, assuming the stumps' thresholds are set with spacing less than the minimum distance between any two points.

title: Ensemble Classifiers and Voting Margin
summary: The ensemble classifier constructed from 2n components has a VC-dimension at least n, indicating its classification power. However, each example in this ensemble has a low voting margin of 1/n. The analysis suggests that ensembles with large voting margins can be approximated by smaller coarse ensembles that classify examples similarly, highlighting the importance of voting margin in understanding ensemble performance beyond VC-dimension.
content: The function hpair(x; x_t, y_t) = sign(y_t(x - x_t + )) + sign(-y_t(x - x_t - )) has value y_t within the interval [x_t - , x_t + ] and is zero elsewhere. Setting \( \alpha_t = 1/n \), the ensemble classifier is defined as \( h_{2n}(x) = \sum_{t=1}^{2n} \alpha_t hpair(x; x_t, y_t) \). This ensemble correctly classifies all training examples and has a VC-dimension of at least n, demonstrating its classification power. However, each example has a low voting margin of 1/n. The analysis proposes refining the understanding of ensemble classifiers by incorporating voting margin, similar to the geometric margin in linear classifiers. Specifically, an ensemble with many components and a large voting margin can be approximated by a smaller coarse ensemble that classifies examples identically, suggesting that voting margin is a key factor in ensemble classifier performance beyond what VC-dimension explains.

relationships.target: Voting margin for coarse ensemble approximation

title: Margin-based Generalization Bound for Ensemble Classifiers
summary: The generalization error of an ensemble classifier can be bounded in terms of the voting margin, the VC-dimension of the base classifiers, and the number of training examples, independent of the number of base classifiers in the ensemble.
content:
With probability at least 1 - \delta over the choice of training data, the generalization error R_n(\hat{h}) of an ensemble classifier \hat{h} satisfies:

R_n(\hat{h}) \leq R_n(\hat{h}; \rho) + \tilde{O}\left(\frac{d_{VC}}{\rho^2 n}\right),

where R_n(\hat{h}; \rho) counts the number of training examples with voting margin less than \rho, d_{VC} is the VC-dimension of the base classifiers, and n is the number of training examples. The bound does not depend on the number of base classifiers in the ensemble. The effective dimension d_{VC}/\rho^2 decreases with increasing margin \rho, implying that larger voting margins allow for smaller ensembles to achieve the same classification error. This result is detailed in Schapire et al. (1998).

title: Mixture Models in Probability
summary: Mixture models are simple and widely used probability models that represent data as a mixture of multiple types, each with its own conditional distribution, capturing ambiguities in observed data.
content: Mixture models are simple probability models designed to capture ambiguities in the available data by mixing different predictions on the probability scale. Given a vector of observations x, a mixture model assumes that x could be of m possible types. If the type j were known, x would be modeled with a conditional distribution P(x|j), such as a Gaussian distribution with a specific mean. The overall frequency of type j in the data is given by P(j). Thus, the mixture model combines these conditional distributions weighted by their frequencies to model the observed data.

title: Mixture Distribution and Mixture of Gaussians Model
summary: A mixture distribution over a variable x is defined as a weighted sum of conditional distributions, representing multiple possible generative processes. Mixture models capture unobserved label information by modeling data as arising from different components, such as in the Naive Bayes model or a two-component Gaussian mixture model.
content:
A mixture distribution over x is given by P(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m P(x|j)P(j), where x can be generated in m possible ways. The generative process involves sampling j from frequencies P(j), then sampling x from the conditional distribution P(x|j). Since the specific generating component j is unobserved, the overall distribution sums over all possibilities weighted by their frequencies.

An example is the Naive Bayes model P(x|y)P(y) over feature vector x and label y. Pooling examples labeled +1 and -1 and ignoring labels yields P(x) = \sum_{y=\pm1} P(x|y)P(y) = \sum_{y=\pm1} \prod_i P(x_i|y) P(y), which assumes examples come from two varieties corresponding to labels. This unobserved label information is what mixture models aim to capture.

A simple two-component mixture of Gaussians model in two dimensions is defined as P(x|\theta) = P(1)N(x; \mu_1, \sigma_1^2 I) + P(2)N(x; \mu_2, \sigma_2^2 I), where parameters \theta include mixing proportions P(1), P(2), means \mu_1, \mu_2, and variances \sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2. This model generates data from two Gaussian components weighted by their mixing frequencies.

title: Mixture Models and Their Application to Clustering and Student Exam Score Prediction
summary: Mixture models generate data by combining multiple components, each with its own mixing proportion, cluster center, and spread, allowing modeling of clusters of varying sizes and locations. They can be applied to predict student exam score vectors by modeling unobserved student types that influence performance across different questions.
content: Mixture models generate data by sampling from multiple components, each characterized by a mixing proportion P(j), which controls the size of the resulting clusters in terms of the number of examples, cluster centers µ_j specifying the location of clusters, and variances σ_j^2 controlling the spread of clusters. Each example in the data could have been generated from any of the mixture components. An application of mixture models is in predicting final exam score vectors for students in machine learning, where each observation x is a vector of points received by a student in particular questions. Different types of students may succeed in different types of questions, but this "student type" information is not directly available in the exam score vectors. Mixture models can be used to model this latent student type information, assuming n students each with a score vector.

title: Mixture Model for Student Types in Exam Scores
summary: A mixture model is used to represent exam score distributions assuming multiple underlying student types, with unknown mixing proportions and types inferred from data.
content: Consider observations x1, ..., xn representing exam scores of n students. There are m underlying types of students, where m can be inferred from the data (a model selection problem). The mixing proportions P(j) for each type j are unknown and must be estimated. The mixture distribution over a single example score vector x is given by P(x|θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(x|j)P(j). The conditional distributions P(x|j) can be parameterized, for example, as P(x|j) = Π_{i=1}^d P(x_i|j) similar to a Naive Bayes model, where each x_i corresponds to scores for exam questions. If the type j_t of each student t were known, the joint distribution of observations would be P(x1,...,xn | j1,...,jn, θ) = Π_{t=1}^n P(x_t | j_t), assuming independence between students. Since type information is not observed, the likelihood sums over all possible type assignments weighted by prior probabilities: P(x1,...,xn | θ) = Π_{t=1}^n Σ_{j=1}^m P(x_t | j) P(j).

title: Difference Between Product-of-Sums and Sum-of-Products Mixture Models
summary: The likelihood of observed data under a mixture model changes significantly depending on whether the model uses a product of sums or a sum of products formulation, leading to different assumptions about the data generation process.
content: The likelihood of the observed data according to a mixture model is given by a product over data points of sums over mixture components: \( P(x_1, ..., x_n | \theta) = \prod_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m P(x_t|j) P(j) \). If we exchange the product and the sum, defining the model as \( P(x_1, ..., x_n | \theta) = \sum_{j=1}^m \prod_{t=1}^n P(x_t|j) P(j) \), we obtain a different mixture model. This alternative model assumes that all data points (students) belong to a single specific type (mixture component), but we do not know which one, summing over the m possible types. In contrast, the original model allows for each data point to be assigned independently to any of the m types, resulting in \( m^n \) possible assignments. Thus, exchanging the product and sum changes the model's assumptions about the data generation process and the number of possible assignments of types to data points.

relationships.target: Difference Between Product-of-Sums and Sum-of-Products Mixture Models

title: Basic Mixture Models and Their Application to Student Exam Scores
summary: Mixture models represent data as a combination of multiple component distributions, capturing observable ambiguities. A Gaussian mixture model with m components is defined by mixing proportions, means, and covariances. Samples are generated by first selecting a component according to the mixing proportions, then sampling from the corresponding Gaussian. This framework can model student exam scores by assuming the population consists of m types of students, each with a probability P(j), and modeling the score distribution as a mixture over these types.
content:
Mixture models aim to capture and resolve observable ambiguities in data by representing the data distribution as a mixture of multiple component distributions. For example, an m-component Gaussian mixture model is given by:

P(x; θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; μ_j, Σ_j)

where θ includes the mixing proportions {P(j)}, means {μ_j}, and covariances {Σ_j} of the component Gaussians. To generate a sample x, one first samples a component index j from the prior distribution {P(j)}, then samples x from the Gaussian N(x; μ_j, Σ_j). Generating n samples results in m potentially overlapping clusters centered at μ_j, with cluster sizes approximately n P(j).

An application is modeling vectors of student exam scores, where each vector x corresponds to a student's scores. The student population is assumed to consist of m types (e.g., due to background differences), each present with probability P(j). The score distribution is modeled as a mixture:

P(x|θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(x|θ_j) P(j)

where the sum is over student types, weighted by their probabilities, reflecting uncertainty about a student's type prior to observing their scores.

title: Likelihood of Student Exam Scores Over Multiple Years Using Mixture Model
summary: This node presents the likelihood function for modeling student exam score vectors over multiple years using a mixture distribution. It assumes a fixed number of student types and score distributions across years, but allows the prior probabilities of types to vary by year.
content:
Given n students in a particular year, the likelihood of all student score vectors D1 = {x1, ..., xn} is:

L(D1; θ) = \prod_{t=1}^n P(x_t|θ) = \prod_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m P(x|θ_j) P(j)

Extending to K years, with n_k students in year k and score vectors x_{k,t}, assuming the number of student types m and distributions P(x|θ_j) remain constant, but prior probabilities P(j|k) vary by year, the mixture distribution for year k is:

P(x|k, θ) = \sum_{j=1}^m P(x|θ_j) P(j|k)

The likelihood of all data across K years, D = {D1, ..., DK}, is:

L(D; θ) = \prod_{k=1}^K \prod_{t=1}^{n_k} P(x_{k,t}|k, θ) = \prod_{k=1}^K \prod_{t=1}^{n_k} \sum_{j=1}^m P(x_{k,t}|θ_j) P(j|k)

title: Collaborative Filtering and Mixture Models in Recommender Systems
summary: Collaborative filtering is a recommender system task where the goal is to predict user ratings for items (e.g., movies) based on observed ratings. Mixture models are applied to this problem by modeling the rating probabilities as mixtures, with parameters including mixing proportions that vary over time.
content:
In recommender systems, collaborative filtering involves predicting missing entries in a user-item rating matrix. Given n users and m movies, each user rates a small subset of movies, and the task is to predict ratings for all user-movie pairs. Ratings rij are integers from 1 to 5, representing the number of stars assigned by user i to movie j.

Mixture models are employed to model the probability of observed ratings. The likelihood function L(D; θ) is given by:

L(D; θ) = ∏_{k=1}^K ∏_{t=1}^{n_k} P(x_{k,t} | k, θ) = ∏_{k=1}^K ∏_{t=1}^{n_k} ∑_{j=1}^m P(x_{k,t} | θ_j) P(j | k)

where θ includes the mixing proportions {P(j | k)} that can change over time (e.g., from year to year), in addition to the component parameters {θ_j}. This formulation allows modeling the collaborative filtering problem as a mixture model, capturing user preferences and item characteristics probabilistically.

title: Mixture Model for Collaborative Filtering with User and Movie Types
summary: A probabilistic mixture model approach to collaborative filtering where each movie and user is represented as a distribution over latent types, and ratings are generated by sampling these types for each rating instance.
content: In collaborative filtering, the observed ratings matrix is partially observed, with (i, j) ∈ ID indicating that user i rated movie j with rating r_ij. The set D denotes all observed ratings. Each movie j is represented by a distribution over movie types z_m ∈ {1, ..., K_m}, and each user i is represented by a distribution over user types z_u ∈ {1, ..., K_u}. Unlike fixed assignments, the model treats these distributions as 'bags of features' from which types are resampled for each rating, allowing different types for different ratings. The rating r_ij is generated by first sampling a movie type from P(z_m | j), then a user type from P(z_u | i), and finally sampling the rating from P(r_ij | z_u, z_m). All probabilities are estimated from data, and the model sums over all unobserved variables without assigning fixed types to ratings. The mixture model for rating r_ij is thus given by the sum over all user and movie types of P(z_u | i) P(z_m | j) P(r_ij | z_u, z_m).

title: Probabilistic Model for Ratings in Collaborative Filtering
summary: This equation represents the probability of a rating given user and item indices and model parameters, decomposed into latent user and item type distributions and rating probabilities conditioned on these types.
content:
P(r_{ij} | i, j, \theta) = \sum_{z_u=1}^{K_u} \sum_{z_m=1}^{K_m} P(r_{ij} | z_u, z_m) P(z_u | i) P(z_m | j)

where \theta includes the parameters mapping types to ratings \{P(r | z_u, z_m)\} and the user- and movie-specific distributions \{P(z_u | i)\} and \{P(z_m | j)\}, respectively.

title: Incorporating User Rating Styles in Movie Rating Prediction Models
summary: The model improves movie rating predictions by introducing user rating styles, where each user is assumed to have a rating style s from a set of possible styles. The likelihood of observed ratings is modified to account for these styles, summing over possible styles for each user.
content:
Users rate movies differently, for example, some use only part of the rating scale (e.g., 3, 4, or 5), while others have bi-modal rating patterns (e.g., 1 or 5). To model this, each user is assumed to have a rating style s ∈ {1, ..., Ks}, common across all users but unknown for each individual. The prior probability that a randomly chosen user has style s is P(s). The rating prediction probabilities now depend on the style s as well: P(r_{ij} | z_u, z_m, s). The likelihood of the observed data D is modified to

L_0(D; θ) = ∏_{i=1}^n ∑_{s=1}^{K_s} P(s) ∏_{j:(i,j)∈I_D} ∑_{z_u=1}^{K_u} ∑_{z_m=1}^{K_m} P(r_{ij} | z_u, z_m, s) P(z_u | i) P(z_m | j)

where all ratings of one user come from one rating style s, but the model sums over possible styles. This approach allows the model to capture different user rating behaviors without greatly increasing the number of parameters to estimate.

title: Parameter Estimation and EM Algorithm in Mixture Models
summary: The model involves a specific number of independent parameters calculated as (Ks − 1) + (5 − 1)KuKmKs + n(Ku − 1) + m(Km − 1). A realistic model also predicts missing elements in the rating matrix by modeling why entries are missing. Mixture models are advantageous for handling ambiguities in data, and their parameters can be estimated using the EM algorithm.
content: The model contains exactly (Ks − 1) + (5 − 1)KuKmKs + n(Ku − 1) + m(Km − 1) independent parameters, corresponding to P(s), P(r|zu,zm,s), P(zu|i), and P(zm|j). A realistic extension includes modeling the missing elements in the rating matrix, accounting for reasons such as a user failing to rate a movie they had seen, not having seen it, or choosing not to see it. Mixture models are beneficial due to their ability to incorporate and resolve ambiguities in data. The EM algorithm is used for estimating parameters in such mixture models.

relationships.target: Modeling missing elements in rating matrix

title: Estimation of Gaussian Mixture Models with Complete Data
summary: Describes the estimation of Gaussian mixture models assuming complete data, where the component assignments for each data point are known, allowing separate estimation of each Gaussian component.
content: The Gaussian mixture model is given by P(x; θ) = \sum_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; \mu_j, \Sigma_j). To simplify estimation, we assume complete data where each observation x_t is accompanied by the component assignment j_t responsible for generating it. This is represented by 0-1 assignments \delta(j|t) where \delta(j_t|t) = 1 and \delta(j|t) = 0 for j \neq j_t. The complete data log-likelihood is l(x_1, ..., x_n, j_1, ..., j_n; \theta) = \sum_{t=1}^n \log P(j_t) N(x_t; \mu_{j_t}, \Sigma_{j_t}) = \sum_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \delta(j|t) \log P(j) N(x_t; \mu_j, \Sigma_j) = \sum_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \delta(j|t) \log P(j) + \sum_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m \delta(j|t) \log N(x_t; \mu_j, \Sigma_j). Because the data is complete, each Gaussian component can be estimated separately from the data points assigned to it, avoiding the problem of determining component responsibility for data points.

title: Parameter Estimation in Gaussian Mixture Models with Known and Unknown Assignments
summary: Describes the closed-form maximum likelihood estimation of Gaussian mixture model parameters when component assignments are known, and the approach to estimate posterior probabilities of component assignments when they are unknown.
content:
When the component assignments j_1, ..., j_n are known, the maximum likelihood estimates of the Gaussian mixture model parameters can be computed in closed form as follows:

- The prior probability for component j is estimated as \( \hat{P}(j) = \frac{\hat{n}(j)}{n} \), where \( \hat{n}(j) = \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t) \) counts the number of data points assigned to component j.

- The mean of component j is estimated as \( \hat{\mu}_j = \frac{1}{\hat{n}(j)} \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t) x_t \).

- The covariance of component j is estimated as \( \hat{\Sigma}_j = \frac{1}{\hat{n}(j)} \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t) (x_t - \hat{\mu}_j)(x_t - \hat{\mu}_j)^T \).

Here, \( \delta(j|t) \) is an indicator function that is 1 if data point \( x_t \) is assigned to component j, and 0 otherwise.

If the assignments are unknown (incomplete data), we can estimate the posterior probability that data point \( x_t \) was generated by component j given current parameters \( \theta^{(l)} \) as:

\[
P^{(l)}(j|x_t) = \frac{P^{(l)}(j) \mathcal{N}(x_t; \mu_j^{(l)}, \Sigma_j^{(l)})}{\sum_{j'=1}^m P^{(l)}(j') \mathcal{N}(x_t; \mu_{j'}^{(l)}, \Sigma_{j'}^{(l)})}
\]

where \( P^{(l)}(j) \), \( \mu_j^{(l)} \), and \( \Sigma_j^{(l)} \) are the current estimates of the mixture weights, means, and covariances respectively, and \( \mathcal{N}(x; \mu, \Sigma) \) denotes the Gaussian density function.

title: Expectation Maximization Algorithm for Gaussian Mixtures
summary: The Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm iteratively estimates parameters of Gaussian mixture models by using soft assignments of data points to components, updating parameters based on current posterior probabilities.
content:
Instead of using hard 0-1 assignments \( \delta(j|t) \) of data points to components, the EM algorithm uses soft assignments \( p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, \theta^{(l)}) \). These soft posterior assignments depend on the current parameter estimates \( \theta^{(l)} \) and are updated iteratively as the parameters are refined. The EM algorithm applies to all mixture models and beyond. For Gaussian mixtures, the algorithm proceeds as follows:

(Step 0) Initialize the Gaussian mixture parameters \( \theta^{(0)} \). A simple initialization sets the mixture weights \( P^{(0)}(j) = 1/m \), assigns each mean \( \mu_j^{(0)} \) to a randomly chosen data point, and sets all covariance matrices \( \Sigma_j^{(0)} \) equal to the overall data covariance.

The iterative nature arises because the soft assignments are computed based on the current parameters and then used to update these parameters, repeating until convergence.

title: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm for Gaussian Mixture Models
summary: The EM algorithm iteratively updates posterior assignment probabilities and parameters of a Gaussian mixture model, guaranteeing non-decreasing log-likelihood and convergence to a local optimum.
content:
The EM algorithm for Gaussian mixture models consists of two steps per iteration:

E-step: Evaluate the posterior assignment probabilities p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, \theta^{(l)}) based on the current parameters \theta^{(l)}.

M-step: Update the parameters as follows:

P^{(l+1)}(j) = \hat{n}(j)/n, where \hat{n}(j) = \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t)

\mu_j^{(l+1)} = \frac{1}{\hat{n}(j)} \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) x_t

\Sigma_j^{(l+1)} = \frac{1}{\hat{n}(j)} \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) (x_t - \mu_j^{(l+1)})(x_t - \mu_j^{(l+1)})^T

This iterative algorithm guarantees that the log-likelihood of the data l(D; \theta^{(l)}) = \sum_{t=1}^n P(x_t; \theta^{(l)}) increases with each iteration until convergence:

l(D; \theta^{(0)}) < l(D; \theta^{(1)}) < l(D; \theta^{(2)}) < ...

However, convergence is only guaranteed to a local optimum where the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to parameters is zero. To mitigate this, the algorithm is typically run multiple times with different random initializations to find a reasonably good solution.

title: EM Algorithm on a Simple Mixture of Two Gaussians
summary: Demonstrates the iterative changes of Gaussian components in a two-Gaussian mixture using the EM algorithm, highlighting soft assignments and convergence behavior.
content: Consider a simple mixture of two Gaussians. The EM algorithm iteratively updates the Gaussian components, as shown in Figure 2, where ellipsoids represent one standard deviation distances from the Gaussian means. The mixing proportions P(j) are not shown. The algorithm requires many iterations to properly assign data points to mixture components. Upon convergence, the assignments remain soft (not binary 0-1) but clearly delineate the responsibilities of the two Gaussian components across data clusters. Note that the highest likelihood for Gaussian mixtures is theoretically infinite, occurring when a Gaussian concentrates on a single data point; such trivial solutions are avoided by constraining covariance matrices or regularization. The meaningful comparison is to non-trivial mixtures achieving the highest log-likelihood.

title: EM Algorithm Example with Two-Component Gaussian Mixture Model
summary: This node presents an example of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm applied to a two-component mixture of Gaussians model, illustrating the initialization and iterations of the algorithm.
content: The figure illustrates the EM algorithm applied to a two-component mixture of Gaussians model. It shows the progression from initialization through iterations 1, 2, 4, 6, and 10. The data points and parameter estimates are represented in a three-dimensional space with coordinates ranging approximately from -0.5 to 2. The example demonstrates how the EM algorithm iteratively updates the parameters of the Gaussian components to fit the data.

title: EM Algorithm for Gaussian Mixture Models
summary: The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is used to estimate parameters of Gaussian mixture models by iteratively performing E and M steps to update posterior assignment probabilities and model parameters.
content:
The Gaussian mixture model is defined as P(x; θ) = \sum_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; µ_j, Σ_j). The EM algorithm estimates the parameters θ by iteratively performing:

E-step: Compute posterior assignment probabilities p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)}) based on current parameters θ^{(l)}.

M-step: Update parameters using:
P^{(l+1)}(j) = \hat{n}(j)/n, where \hat{n}(j) = \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t),
µ_j^{(l+1)} = (1/\hat{n}(j)) \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) x_t,
Σ_j^{(l+1)} = (1/\hat{n}(j)) \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) (x_t - µ_j^{(l+1)})(x_t - µ_j^{(l+1)})^T.

title: Initialization Sensitivity of the EM Algorithm in Gaussian Mixture Models
summary: The EM algorithm for Gaussian mixture models is sensitive to parameter initialization because identical initial parameters lead to identical posterior assignments and updates, causing the algorithm to estimate effectively a single Gaussian. To avoid degenerate solutions, sufficient variation in initialization, such as random placement of component means, is necessary, and multiple runs are recommended to find good solutions.
content: The EM algorithm is iterative and can get stuck in locally optimal solutions, making parameter initialization critical. If all Gaussian components are initialized with identical means and covariances, their posterior probabilities remain identical, resulting in identical parameter updates and effectively estimating only a single Gaussian distribution. This degeneracy occurs even if prior probabilities differ but component models are identical. To prevent this, sufficient variation in initialization is required. For example, mixing proportions can be uniform (P^{(0)}(j) = 1/m) and covariance matrices can equal the overall data covariance, but the Gaussian component means should be randomly positioned, such as by selecting random data points. Despite such initialization, multiple runs of the EM algorithm are necessary to increase the chance of finding a good solution. Figure 1 illustrates a locally optimal solution with four Gaussian components obtained from a four-component mixture dataset.

title: EM Algorithm for General Mixture Models
summary: The EM algorithm is applied to a general mixture model to maximize the log-likelihood of observed data by iteratively computing expected complete log-likelihood using soft posterior assignments.
content:
Consider a general mixture model defined as P(x; θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(j) P(x|θ_j), where θ includes both the mixture weights {P(j)} and component parameters {θ_j}. Given data D = {x_1, ..., x_n}, the goal is to maximize the log-likelihood l(D; θ) = Σ_{t=1}^n log P(x_t; θ).

Assuming complete data with known assignments J = {j_1, ..., j_n}, the complete log-likelihood is l(D, J; θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m Σ_{t=1}^n δ(j|t) log P(j) P(x_t|θ_j), where δ(j|t) = 1 if j = j_t and 0 otherwise.

In the EM algorithm, at iteration l with current parameters θ^{(l)}, the E-step replaces hard assignments δ(j|t) with soft posterior assignments p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)}). This leads to the expected complete log-likelihood E[l(D, J; θ) | D, θ^{(l)}] = Σ_{j=1}^m Σ_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) log P(j) P(x_t|θ_j).

title: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm: E-step and M-step Explanation
summary: The EM algorithm addresses incomplete data problems by iteratively performing an E-step, which computes the expected assignments of latent variables given current parameters, and an M-step, which optimizes parameters based on these completed data assignments.
content: The expectation in the EM algorithm is computed over the assignments given the observed data D = {x1, ..., xn} and the current parameter setting θ(l). Specifically, the expectation E l(D, J ; θ) is expressed as \( \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) \log P(j) P(x_t|\theta_j) \), where \( p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, \theta^{(l)}) \) represents the posterior probability of assignment j for data point t under current parameters. The E-step averages over unknown variable assignments relative to the current model, effectively completing the incomplete observations. Two parameter sets are involved: the current parameters θ(l) used to compute posterior assignments, and θ, which is optimized in the M-step. Once posterior assignments \( p^{(l)}(j|t) \) are evaluated, they remain fixed with respect to θ during the M-step. Thus, the E-step transforms the incomplete data problem into a complete data problem, enabling parameter optimization in the M-step.

title: EM Algorithm as Optimization of an Auxiliary Objective
summary: The EM algorithm maximizes the expected log-likelihood with respect to parameters θ by treating observed data and soft completions as fixed, optimizing an auxiliary objective that provides a lower bound on the log-likelihood, thereby increasing it from below.
content: Given observed data D = {x1, ..., xn} and soft completions p^{(l)}(j|t), the EM algorithm maximizes the expected log-likelihood with respect to parameters θ while keeping other variables fixed. The algorithm optimizes an auxiliary objective function defined over any set of distributions Q = {q(j|t)} on the latent assignments, not necessarily the posterior p^{(l)}(j|t). This auxiliary objective forces the log-likelihood l(D; θ) to increase from below, ensuring convergence towards a local maximum.

title: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm Objective and Steps
summary: The EM algorithm maximizes the objective function l(D, Q; θ) by alternating between optimizing the assignment distributions Q (E-step) and the parameters θ (M-step). The assignment distributions Q are set to the posterior probabilities P(j|x, θ) in the E-step, and the parameters θ are updated in the M-step to maximize the objective given Q.
content:
The objective function for the EM algorithm is defined as:

l(D, Q; θ) = \sum_{t=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m q(j|t) \log P(j) P(x|θ_j) + \sum_{t=1}^n H(q(·|t))

where H(q(·|t)) = - \sum_{j=1}^m q(j|t) \log q(j|t) is the entropy of the assignment distribution q(·|t). The function l(D, Q; θ) is viewed as a function of Q and θ, with q(j|t) representing assignment distributions that can be set independently of θ.

The EM algorithm alternates between:

- E-step: For fixed θ^(l), find Q^(l) = arg max_Q l(D, Q; θ^(l)), which corresponds to setting q^(l)(j|t) = p^(l)(j|t) = P(j|x, θ^(l)), the posterior assignments.

- M-step: For fixed Q^(l), update parameters θ^(l+1) = arg max_θ l(D, Q^(l); θ).

It can be shown that l(D, Q; θ^(l)) is maximized with respect to Q exactly when Q equals the posterior distributions Q^(l). Thus, the EM algorithm iteratively recovers posterior assignments in the E-step and maximizes the objective with respect to parameters in the M-step.

relationships.target: assignment distributions Q as posterior probabilities P(j|x, θ)

title: EM Algorithm Objective and Monotone Increase of Log-Likelihood
summary: The EM algorithm alternates between an E-step that recovers posterior assignments and an M-step that maximizes an auxiliary objective function, ensuring a monotone increase in the log-likelihood.
content:
The E-step recovers the posterior assignments q^{(l)}(j|t) = p^{(l)}(j|t). The M-step maximizes the auxiliary objective function:

l(D, Q^{(l)}; \theta) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) \log P(j)P(x|\theta_j) + \sum_{t=1}^n H(p^{(l)}(\cdot|t))

where the entropy term H(p^{(l)}(\cdot|t)) is fixed during optimization of \theta. Each step is a maximization step, so the objective l(D, Q; \theta) increases monotonically. This monotone increase underlies the monotone increase of the log-likelihood l(D; \theta) in the EM algorithm. The auxiliary objective equals the log-likelihood after any E-step:

l(D, Q^{(l)}; \theta^{(l)}) = l(D; \theta^{(l)})

title: Derivation of the EM Algorithm Auxiliary Function and Monotonic Likelihood Increase
summary: This node presents the step-by-step derivation showing that the auxiliary function l(D, Q(l); θ(l)) used in the EM algorithm satisfies the inequality chain ensuring monotonic increase of the data log-likelihood l(D;θ) across EM iterations. The derivation highlights the necessity of the entropy term in the auxiliary objective and culminates in the inequality l(D;θ(l)) ≤ l(D;θ(l+1)) ≤ ... demonstrating the EM algorithm's convergence property.
content:
The derivation begins by substituting the posterior assignments p^{(l)}(j|t) into the auxiliary function l(D, Q^{(l)}; θ^{(l)}):

l(D, Q^{(l)}; θ^{(l)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) \log P^{(l)}(j) P(x_t|θ_j^{(l)}) + \sum_{t=1}^n H(p^{(l)}(·|t))

Expanding the entropy term H(p^{(l)}(·|t)) and rearranging terms yields:

= \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) \log P^{(l)}(j) P(x_t|θ_j^{(l)}) - \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(j|t) \log p^{(l)}(j|t)

Recognizing that p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)}), the expression simplifies to:

= \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)}) \log \frac{P^{(l)}(j) P(x_t|θ_j^{(l)})}{P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)})}

= \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{t=1}^n P(j|x_t, θ^{(l)}) \log P(x_t; θ^{(l)})

= \sum_{t=1}^n \log P(x_t; θ^{(l)}) = l(D; θ^{(l)})

This shows that the auxiliary function equals the data log-likelihood at the current parameter estimate θ^{(l)}. The entropy term is essential for this equality.

Finally, the EM algorithm guarantees the following monotonic increase in the log-likelihood:

l(D; θ^{(l)}) = l(D, Q^{(l)}; θ^{(l)}) ≤ l(D, Q^{(l)}; θ^{(l+1)}) ≤ l(D, Q^{(l+1)}; θ^{(l+1)}) ≤ ...

This chain of inequalities ensures that each EM iteration does not decrease the data log-likelihood, demonstrating convergence behavior.

title: Regularization in Gaussian Mixture Models and EM Algorithm
summary: Regularization is important in flexible models like Gaussian mixture models, especially when the number of parameters grows large with the number of components and dimensions. Incorporating regularization requires revising the EM algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, affecting the update equations similarly to the complete data case, with posterior probabilities replacing the δ(j|t) terms.
content: In a mixture of Gaussians model with m components in d dimensions, the number of parameters is m - 1 + md + md(d + 1)/2, which can become large when m or d is large. Regularization is crucial to control model complexity in such flexible models. To include regularization, the basic EM algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation must be revised. The effect of regularization on the update equations is analogous to the complete data case, with the δ(j|t) terms replaced by posterior probabilities. Additionally, the EM algorithm monotonically increases the log-likelihood, with equality holding only at convergence.

title: Regularization of Covariance Matrices Using Wishart Prior in Complete Data Settings
summary: This method describes regularizing covariance matrices in a model with complete observations by assigning a Wishart prior, which is conjugate and facilitates estimation. The prior depends on a common covariance matrix S and an equivalent sample size n0 that controls the strength of the prior's influence relative to the data. The penalized complete log-likelihood incorporates the Wishart prior penalty, modifying the estimation of covariance matrices accordingly.
content:
In a setting with complete observations, covariance matrices Σ_j are regularized by assigning a Wishart prior, a conjugate prior over covariance matrices. The prior depends on two parameters: a common covariance matrix S, towards which the estimates of Σ_j are pulled, and an equivalent sample size n_0, which specifies the number of data points needed for the data to influence the solution as much as the prior. The log-Wishart penalty is given by:

log P(Σ_j | S, n_0) = const. - n_0/2 * Trace(Σ_j^{-1} S) - n_0/2 * log |Σ_j|

Given data D = {x_1, ..., x_n} and assignments J = {j_1, ..., j_n}, the penalized complete log-likelihood function is:

l(D, J; θ) = Σ_{j=1}^m Σ_{t=1}^n δ(j|t) log P(j) + Σ_{j=1}^m Σ_{t=1}^n δ(j|t) log N(x_t; μ_j, Σ_j) + log P(Σ_j | S, n_0)

The estimation solution changes slightly, affecting only the covariance matrices due to the prior.

title: Covariance Matrix Updates in EM Algorithm with Regularization
summary: Describes the update rules for covariance matrices in the EM algorithm incorporating a regularization term corresponding to prior observations with covariance S.
content:
The covariance matrix update in the EM algorithm is given by:

nˆ(j) = \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t)

\muˆ_j = \frac{1}{nˆ(j)} \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t) x_t

\Sigmaˆ_j = \frac{1}{nˆ(j) + n_0} \left[ \sum_{t=1}^n \delta(j|t) (x_t - \muˆ_j)(x_t - \muˆ_j)^T + n_0 S \right]

where \delta(j|t) are the posterior assignments p^{(l)}(j|t) in the EM algorithm. The regularization term n_0 S corresponds to having observed n_0 samples with covariance S from the same Gaussian. The choice of S depends on the problem and can be, for example, the identity matrix or the overall data covariance \Sigma. This update rule is not expressed in terms of inverse covariance matrices as would be the case when combining noisy sources with different noise covariances.

relationships.target: Regularization term n_0 S corresponds to prior observations with covariance S

title: Sequential Estimation of Mixture Models via EM Algorithm
summary: Sequential estimation of mixture models involves adding components one at a time to an existing mixture model, estimating the new component's parameters and weight using the EM algorithm, which simplifies the estimation problem compared to estimating the full mixture at once.
content: Mixture models serve two purposes: providing efficiently parameterized densities over x and uncovering data structure by identifying group memberships. Focusing on predicting x, mixture models can be estimated sequentially, similarly to boosting. Given an existing mixture model with m-1 components, \( \hat{P}_{m-1}(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} \hat{P}(j) P(x|\hat{\theta}_j) \), a new m-component mixture is parameterized as \( P(x; p_m, \theta_m) = (1 - p_m) \hat{P}_{m-1}(x) + p_m P(x|\theta_m) = \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} [(1 - p_m) \hat{P}(j)] P(x|\hat{\theta}_j) + p_m P(x|\theta_m) \). Scaling down \( \hat{P}_{m-1}(x) \) by \( 1 - p_m \) ensures mixture proportions sum to one for any \( p_m \in [0,1] \). The parameters \( p_m \) and \( \theta_m \) of the new component are estimated via the EM algorithm, which is simpler than estimating the full mixture since only one component and its weight are adjusted. The E-step involves evaluating posterior assignment probabilities for the new component.

title: EM Algorithm Parameter Update Steps
summary: Describes the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm steps for updating posterior assignment probabilities and parameters of mixture components.
content:
The EM algorithm consists of two main steps for parameter estimation in mixture models:

E-step: Evaluate the posterior assignment probabilities for the new component m at iteration l:

p^{(l)}(m|t) = \frac{p_m^{(l)} P(x_t|\theta_m^{(l)})}{(1 - p_m^{(l)}) \hat{P}^{m-1}(x_t) + p_m^{(l)} P(x_t|\theta_m^{(l)})}

M-step: Update the parameters p_m and \theta_m for the next iteration (l+1):

p_m^{(l+1)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(m|t)

\theta_m^{(l+1)} = \arg\max_{\theta_m} \sum_{t=1}^n p^{(l)}(m|t) \log P(x_t|\theta_m)

where n is the number of data points, p_m^{(l)} is the mixture weight, \theta_m^{(l)} are the parameters of component m at iteration l, and P(x_t|\theta_m) is the likelihood of data point x_t given parameters \theta_m.

title: Conditional Mixture Models for Regression (Mixtures of Experts)
summary: Conditional mixture models, also known as mixtures of experts, are used for regression tasks where the response variable is predicted as a function of the input. These models replace hard assignments with soft posterior assignments and often require regularization of mixture components. They can model non-linear response functions by combining multiple linear regression experts weighted by a gating network.
content: Conditional mixture models (mixtures of experts) apply mixture modeling to regression problems. The model assumes a simple linear regression for each expert: P(y|x, θ, σ²) = N(y; θᵀx, σ²). However, when responses are not linear functions of the input, multiple experts are combined. The hard assignments δ(m|t) used in standard mixture models are replaced by soft posterior assignments p^(l)(m|t), maximizing the expected log-likelihood (Eq. 29). This approach parallels the updates used in Gaussian mixtures. Regularization of mixture components is often necessary, even when components are added sequentially. The gating network outputs probabilities that select among experts, and the overall mean output is a function of the input, representing the conditional mixture distribution. Figure 2 illustrates: (a) a regression problem, (b) linear regression experts and their assigned regions, (c) gating network output probabilities, and (d) mean output from the conditional mixture distribution as a function of input.

title: Conditional Mixture Models with Gating Networks for Non-linear Regression
summary: Conditional mixture models use gating networks to assign linear expert models to different regions of the input space, enabling modeling of non-linear relationships between input x and output y. The gating network predicts mixing proportions conditioned on x, and the overall response model is a mixture of linear Gaussian components weighted by these proportions. The model parameters can be estimated using the EM algorithm, where the E-step computes posterior assignment probabilities based on both inputs and outputs.
content:
To capture non-linear relationships between input x and output y, one approach is to divide the input space into regions where the relation can be approximated by linear functions. Conditional mixture models implement this by assigning linear expert models to regions via a gating network. The gating network predicts the mixing proportions P(j|x, η, η0), for example using logistic regression: P(j=1|x, η, η0) = g(η^T x + η0), and for multiple regions a softmax function is used. The overall conditional model for y given x is:

P(y|x) = Σ_j P(j|x, η, η0) N(y; θ_j^T x, σ_j^2)

This differs from simple mixture models as both mixing proportions and component models depend on x. Parameter estimation can be performed via the EM algorithm, where the E-step computes posterior assignment probabilities p^{(l)}(j|t) = P(j|x_t, η^{(l)}, η_0^{(l)}) N(y_t; (θ^{(l)})^T x_t, (σ^{(l)})^2) / P^{(l)}(y_t|x_t), incorporating both input and output data.

title: M-step Parameter Estimation in Mixture of Experts Model
summary: The M-step in the EM algorithm updates parameters by maximizing expected log-likelihoods with respect to posterior assignments, specifically updating mixture weights and regression parameters in the mixture of experts model.
content: In the M-step of the EM algorithm for the mixture of experts model, new parameters are obtained by maximizing the expected log-likelihoods relative to the posterior assignments. Specifically, the mixture weights {η(l+1), η(l+1)_0} are updated by maximizing the sum over data points and mixture components of the posterior probabilities p^(l)(j|t) times the log of the mixture component probabilities P(j|x_t, η, η_0), as shown in equation (34). Similarly, the regression parameters {θ_j^(l+1), σ_j^(l+1)} are updated by maximizing the sum over data points of the posterior probabilities times the log of the Gaussian likelihood N(y_t; θ_j^T x_t, σ_j^2), as shown in equation (35). These estimation equations are derived from the complete log-likelihood by replacing the indicator δ(j|t) with the posterior assignments p^(l)(j|t). Figure 2 in the source illustrates the resulting mixture of experts model applied to a toy problem.

title: Mixture Models for Clustering with Spherical Gaussian Components
summary: Mixture models can be used not only for prediction but also for uncovering latent group structures in data, a task known as clustering. A common approach is to model data as a mixture of spherical Gaussian clusters, estimating parameters such as mixing proportions, means, and variances. Key challenges include determining the number of clusters, data sufficiency for identification, algorithmic robustness, and model selection.
content:
Mixture models have been used as flexible probability models for prediction tasks by incorporating unobserved subgroups in the data. This leads to clustering problems where the goal is to uncover the latent group structure within the data. For example, identifying types of students based on exam scores or determining gene expression patterns in mixed cell-type tissue samples. The simplest clustering approach involves modeling data as a mixture of spherical Gaussian clusters, expressed as:

P(x; θ, m) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; μ_j, σ_j^2 I)

where θ includes the mixing proportions P(j), means μ_j, and variances σ_j^2. The focus is on locating clusters rather than optimizing the generative model fit. Important questions include how many spherical Gaussian clusters exist (a model selection problem), whether there is enough data to identify them, the feasibility of finding clusters via the EM algorithm, and the robustness of the clustering method in the presence of background samples or impurities. Enhancing robustness is also a consideration.

title: Mixture Models and Clustering
summary: Mixture models are used both for constructing probability models for prediction and for uncovering unobserved subgroup structures in data, which is the clustering problem. Different clustering algorithms exist, such as hierarchical agglomerative clustering and k-means, each suitable for different purposes. Mixture models as generative models require specifying the type of clusters, with spherical Gaussian clusters being a simple example modeled by Gaussian mixtures.
content: Mixture models have been used as flexible probability models for prediction tasks, motivated by the presence of unobserved subgroups in data. Incorporating such subgroup structure improves prediction accuracy and enables uncovering the group structure, known as clustering. Clustering problems arise in various contexts, such as identifying student types from exam scores or determining gene expression in cell types from tissue samples. Various clustering algorithms exist: hierarchical agglomerative clustering generates nested clusters by merging smaller ones, while methods like k-means find a pre-specified number of clusters that best capture the data. The choice of algorithm depends on the clustering goal, so knowledge of multiple methods is useful. Mixture models as generative models require articulating the cluster types sought. The simplest clusters are spherical Gaussian clusters, modeled by Gaussian mixtures of the form P(x; θ, m) = Σ_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; μ_j, σ_j^2 I).

title: Gaussian Mixture Model with Spherical Clusters
summary: Defines a Gaussian mixture model with spherical Gaussian clusters and discusses challenges in model selection and cluster identification using the EM algorithm.
content: P(x; \theta, m) = \sum_{j=1}^m P(j) N(x; \mu_j, \sigma_j^2 I) where \theta = \{P(j), \mu_j, \sigma_j^2\}. The focus is on identifying cluster locations rather than the generative quality of the mixture model. Key questions include determining the number of spherical Gaussian clusters (model selection), data sufficiency for cluster identification, the feasibility of using the EM algorithm to find clusters, and the robustness of the method.

title: Simplified Gaussian Mixture Model for Clustering with Identical Covariances and Uniform Mixing Proportions
summary: The text discusses the use of Gaussian mixture models for clustering, highlighting issues when variances differ across spherical Gaussian components, and introduces a simplified mixture model with identical covariance matrices and uniform mixing proportions to better align with clustering goals.
content:
In clustering using Gaussian mixture models, when variances of spherical Gaussian components differ, points far from cluster means tend to be assigned to the Gaussian with the larger variance due to slower tail decay, which may not align with clustering objectives. To address this and simplify analysis, the covariance matrices are restricted to be identical and equal to \( \sigma^2 I \), where \( \sigma^2 \) is common to all clusters. Additionally, mixing proportions are fixed to be uniform, \( P(j) = 1/m \), where \( m \) is the number of clusters. The resulting simplified mixture model is given by:

\[
P(x; \theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{j=1}^m N(x; \mu_j, \sigma^2 I)
\]

This model facilitates understanding the types of clusters discovered and avoids issues related to differing variances in Gaussian components.

title: Cluster Assignment Boundaries in EM Algorithm for Gaussian Mixture Models
summary: In the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixture models with equal prior probabilities and spherical covariance matrices, the space is partitioned into regions where each component has the highest posterior probability. The boundary between two components i and j is defined by points where their posterior probabilities are equal, which occurs when the Euclidean distances from the point to the component means are equal.
content: The mixture model partitions the space into regions where each Gaussian component has the highest posterior probability. Considering two components i and j, the boundary where P(i|x, θ) = P(j|x, θ) is the set of points equidistant from their means, since the Gaussians have equal prior probabilities and identical spherical covariance matrices σ²I. This equality implies N(x; µ_j, σ²I) = N(x; µ_i, σ²I), which leads to the condition kx - µ_i k² = kx - µ_j k² or equivalently 2x^T(µ_j - µ_i) = ||µ_j||² - ||µ_i||². Thus, the posterior probabilities are equal on the hyperplane equidistant from the two means, defining the cluster assignment boundary in the EM algorithm.

title: Voronoi Partition and K-means Algorithm in EM Clustering
summary: The EM algorithm's E-step computes posterior assignment probabilities that induce a Voronoi partition of the space based on closest means, with boundaries linear in x when Gaussians share the same covariance. The variance parameter σ² controls the sharpness of posterior transitions across boundaries. The K-means algorithm simplifies EM by assigning points to the closest mean and updating means as centroids of assigned points, iteratively redefining Voronoi regions.
content:
In the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixture models with equal covariance matrices, the decision boundaries between components are linear in the input space x. These boundaries form a Voronoi partition where each region corresponds to points closest to a particular mean µ_j. The posterior assignment probabilities P(j|x, θ) computed in the E-step do not vanish at boundaries but indicate which component has the highest posterior probability. The variance parameter σ² controls the sharpness of transitions in posterior probabilities across boundaries: smaller σ² yields sharper transitions, larger σ² smoother changes.

The K-means algorithm is a simplified and faster version of EM clustering. It assigns each data point x_t to the component with the closest mean µ_j (jt = arg min_j ||x_t - µ_j||²), effectively assigning points within each Voronoi region to one component. The M-step updates each mean µ_j to the centroid of points assigned to it. This process iterates, redefining Voronoi regions and updating means until convergence.

Note: The linearity of boundaries holds when the Gaussian components have the same covariance matrix, spherical or not.

title: K-means Algorithm as a Hard Assignment EM Algorithm
summary: The K-means algorithm is a hard assignment version of the EM algorithm that optimizes the complete log-likelihood by alternating between assigning data points to clusters (E-step) and updating cluster means (M-step), minimizing the overall squared error (distortion). It converges in a finite number of steps to locally optimal cluster means and is sensitive to initialization, for which a greedy packing algorithm is commonly used.
content:
The K-means algorithm can be viewed as optimizing the complete log-likelihood of the data with respect to cluster assignments j_1, ..., j_n (E-step) and cluster means μ_1, ..., μ_m (M-step). This optimization is equivalent to minimizing the overall squared error (distortion) to the cluster means:

J(j_1, ..., j_n, μ_1, ..., μ_m) = Σ_{t=1}^n ||x_t - μ_{j_t}||^2

Each E-step or M-step decreases the objective until convergence. The algorithm cannot revisit the same assignments as that would yield the same objective value. Since there are O(n^k) possible partitions with k means, convergence occurs in a finite number of steps. At convergence, the cluster means μ̂_1, ..., μ̂_m are locally optimal solutions to the minimum distortion objective:

J(μ̂_1, ..., μ̂_m) = Σ_{t=1}^n min_j ||x_t - μ̂_j||^2

The K-means algorithm is faster but more sensitive to initialization than a Gaussian mixture model trained with EM. A typical initialization is a greedy packing algorithm: the first mean is a randomly selected training point, the second is the furthest training point from the first mean, the third is the furthest from the two means, and so forth.

relationships.target: minimizing overall squared error (distortion) to cluster means
mixture of Gaussians trained with EM

title: Identifiability in k-means and Gaussian Mixture Models with EM
summary: Identifiability refers to the ability of k-means or Gaussian mixture models using the EM algorithm to recover the maximum likelihood solution, which depends on the number of training examples and affects clustering quality and difficulty.
content: The k-means algorithm and Gaussian mixture models optimized via the EM algorithm can only achieve the quality of the maximum likelihood solution they aim to recover. Even when the underlying clusters are spherical, if the number of training examples is too small, the globally optimal (non-trivial) maximum likelihood solution may not yield reasonable clusters. As the number of data points increases, the quality of the maximum likelihood solution improves, but finding this solution with the EM algorithm can remain challenging. A larger number of training points also facilitates finding the maximum likelihood solution. Thus, the clustering problem can be roughly divided into three regimes based on the number of training points: not solvable, solvable but hard, and easy. For further discussion on these regimes, see Srebro et al., “An Investigation of Computational and Informational Limits in Gaussian Mixture Clustering”, ICML 2006.

title: Role of Distance Metrics in Clustering and TFIDF Feature Representation
summary: This concept discusses the importance of distance metrics in clustering algorithms, particularly the use of Euclidean distance in Gaussian mixture models and K-means. It highlights that the choice of distance metric depends on the feature representation, exemplified by document clustering using TFIDF vectors. The TFIDF mapping transforms documents into feature vectors by weighting term frequencies with inverse document frequency to reduce the impact of common words. The concept also notes that hierarchical agglomerative clustering relies heavily on the distance function to merge clusters.
content:
Gaussian mixture models and the K-means algorithm utilize the Euclidean distance between points for clustering. However, the appropriateness of Euclidean distance depends on the feature representation of the objects, which often results from feature transformations. For example, in document clustering, each document x can be represented as a bag of words and mapped into a feature vector φ(x) using the TFIDF mapping. The TFIDF features are computed as follows:

nw(x) = number of times word w appears in document x
f(w|x) = nw(x) / Σ_{w'} nw'(x)  (term frequency)
φw(x) = f(w|x) · log(# of documents / # of documents containing word w)  (TFIDF feature)

The inverse document frequency (IDF) component downweights words that appear in many documents, which are less informative for clustering or classification. These TFIDF vectors can be interpreted as points in Euclidean space, allowing the application of algorithms like K-means. Nonetheless, alternative distance metrics may be more suitable depending on the data and feature representation.

Distance metrics are central to clustering algorithms in general. For instance, hierarchical agglomerative clustering is defined primarily by the distance function, proceeding by iteratively merging the two closest points or clusters based on average squared distance.

title: Role of Distance Metric in Clustering and Model-Based Distance Definition
summary: Distance metrics are fundamental to clustering algorithms, such as hierarchical agglomerative clustering, which merges closest points or clusters based on average squared distance. Defining an appropriate distance (similarity) metric is crucial and can be approached via model selection, exemplified by using a unigram model for documents where words are independent samples from a multinomial distribution.
content: Distance metric plays a central role in clustering, regardless of the algorithm. For example, a simple hierarchical agglomerative clustering algorithm is defined almost entirely on the basis of the distance function. The algorithm proceeds by successively merging two closest points or closest clusters (average squared distance). In solving clustering problems, the focus should be on defining the distance (similarity) metric, perhaps at the expense of a specific algorithm, since most algorithms could be applied with the chosen metric. One avenue for defining a distance metric is through model selection. The simplest model over the words in a document is a unigram model where each word is an independent sample from a multinomial distribution {θ_w}, with ∑_w θ_w = 1. The probability of all the words in document x is therefore P(x|θ) = ∏_{w∈x} θ_w^{n_w(x)}.

title: Normalization and Unigram Model Estimation in Hierarchical Clustering
summary: Describes the normalization of documents to unit length using term frequencies and the estimation of the unigram model parameters for a cluster by maximizing log-likelihood based on normalized documents.
content: In hierarchical clustering of documents, it is often beneficial to normalize documents so that they have the same length, for example, by setting each document length to one and representing word counts by term frequencies f(w|x). The probability of a normalized document \( \tilde{x} \) given parameters \( \theta \) is modeled as \( P(\tilde{x}|\theta) = \prod_w \theta_w^{f(w|x)} \). For a cluster of documents \( C \), the unigram model parameters \( \theta \) that best describe the normalized documents are obtained by maximizing the log-likelihood \( l(C; \theta) = \sum_{x \in C} \sum_w f(w|x) \log \theta_w \). The maximum likelihood estimate of \( \theta_w \) is given by the empirical average of term frequencies over the cluster: \( \hat{\theta}_w = \frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{x \in C} f(w|x) \).

title: Log-likelihood and entropy in unigram clustering model
summary: The log-likelihood of a cluster under a unigram model is expressed in terms of the entropy of the unigram distribution. A model selection approach is used to decide whether to merge two clusters by comparing log-likelihoods of separate versus combined unigram models.
content:
The log-likelihood value for a cluster C under unigram model parameters \( \hat{\theta} \) is given by:

\[
l(C; \hat{\theta}) = \sum_{x \in C} \sum_w f(w|x) \log \hat{\theta}_w = |C| \sum_w \hat{\theta}_w \log \hat{\theta}_w = -|C| H(\hat{\theta})
\]

where \( H(\hat{\theta}) \) is the entropy of the unigram distribution.

For two clusters \( C_i \) and \( C_j \), with combined cluster \( C = C_i \cup C_j \), separate unigram models \( \hat{\theta}_{\cdot|i} \) and \( \hat{\theta}_{\cdot|j} \) are used for \( C_i \) and \( C_j \) respectively, while a single model is used for the combined cluster.

The log-likelihood when clusters are modeled separately is:

\[
l(C_i|\hat{\theta}_{\cdot|i}) + l(C_j|\hat{\theta}_{\cdot|j}) = -|C_i| H(\hat{\theta}_{\cdot|i}) - |C_j| H(\hat{\theta}_{\cdot|j}) = -(|C_i| + |C_j|) \sum_{y \in \{i,j\}} \hat{P}(y) H(\hat{\theta}_{\cdot|y})
\]

This formulation enables a model selection problem to decide whether to merge clusters based on log-likelihood comparisons.

title: Log-Likelihood Ratio Statistic for Measuring Distance Between Clusters
summary: Defines a squared distance measure between two clusters based on the improvement in modeling them as separate clusters using log-likelihood ratio statistics, involving cluster size weighted parameter estimates and entropy.
content: Given two clusters Ci and Cj with y ∈ {i, j}, the probability that a randomly drawn document from C = Ci ∪ Cj belongs to cluster Ci is Pˆ(y = i) = |Ci| / (|Ci| + |Cj|). Parameter estimates θˆw|i and θˆw|j are obtained for each cluster. When modeling both clusters with the same unigram model, the log-likelihood is l(Ci, Cj | θˆ) = -(|Ci| + |Cj|) H(θˆ), where θˆw = Σ_{y∈{i,j}} Pˆ(y) θˆw|y, a cluster size weighted combination of individual cluster estimates. The squared distance between Ci and Cj is defined as the log-likelihood ratio statistic: d²(Ci, Cj) = l(Ci | θˆ·|i) + l(Cj | θˆ·|j) - l(Ci, Cj | θˆ) = (|Ci| + |Cj|) H(θˆ) - Σ_{y∈{i,j}} Pˆ(y) H(θˆ·|y) = (|Ci| + |Cj|) Î(w; y), where H denotes entropy and Î(w; y) is the estimated mutual information between word distributions and cluster labels.

relationships.target: log-likelihood ratio statistic d²(Ci, Cj) as a measure of cluster distance

title: Mutual Information-Based Cluster Distance Metric in Hierarchical Clustering
summary: The squared metric d2(Ci, Cj) measures the distinguishability of two clusters Ci and Cj based on the mutual information between words sampled from their combined cluster and the cluster identity. It is symmetric and non-negative but not necessarily a metric. This metric can be used in hierarchical clustering algorithms, such as the agglomerative information bottleneck method, to compare clusters and decide when to stop merging.
content: The squared distance metric d2(Ci, Cj) is defined using the mutual information Iˆ(w; y) between words w sampled from the combined cluster C = Ci ∪ Cj and the cluster identity y (either i or j). The mutual information is computed based on the joint distribution Pˆ(w, y) = Pˆ(y)θˆw|y, where θˆw|y represents the word distribution conditioned on cluster y. This metric is symmetric and non-negative but does not necessarily satisfy all metric properties. It quantifies how distinguishable the two clusters are by measuring how much information a randomly sampled word from the combined cluster provides about which cluster it originated from. Low mutual information indicates nearly identical word distributions between clusters. The squared metric d2(Ci, Cj) can be directly applied in hierarchical clustering algorithms, including the agglomerative information bottleneck method, to compare clusters and potentially guide model selection decisions such as when to stop merging clusters.

title: Spectral Clustering and Graph Construction
summary: Spectral clustering is a class of clustering methods that approximate partitioning nodes in a weighted graph as eigenvalue problems, where the graph represents similarities between objects. The weighted graph is constructed typically using a k-nearest neighbor approach with edge weights defined by an exponential function of the distance between points.
content:
Spectral clustering refers to a class of clustering methods that approximate the problem of partitioning nodes in a weighted graph as eigenvalue problems. The weighted graph represents a similarity matrix between the objects associated with the nodes in the graph. A large positive weight connecting any two nodes (high similarity) biases the clustering algorithm to place the nodes in the same cluster. The graph representation is relational in the sense that it only holds information about the comparison of objects associated with the nodes.

Graph construction:
A relational representation can be advantageous even when a vector space representation is available. For example, points that form clusters not well captured by spherical Gaussians can be represented by connecting each point to its two nearest neighbors, yielding a graph that places clusters in different connected components. This relational representation can identify clusters along lower dimensional surfaces (manifolds) rather than in the enclosing space.

To construct the weighted graph, a typical method is to build a k-nearest neighbor graph: an undirected graph over n points where nodes i and j are connected if i is among the k nearest neighbors of j or vice versa. The edge weights are set as:

\[ W_{ij} = \begin{cases} \exp(-\beta \|x_i - x_j\|) & \text{if } i \text{ and } j \text{ are connected} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The resulting weights are symmetric, i.e., \( W_{ij} = W_{ji} \).

title: k-Nearest Neighbor Graph Construction and Parameter Selection
summary: The construction of a weighted k-nearest neighbor graph involves setting diagonal entries to zero and choosing parameters k and β, where k relates to the dimensionality of clusters and β to the scale of point distances. A small k leads to a sparse graph limiting comparisons to nearby points, which is beneficial when Euclidean distance is a reasonable approximation only for close points.
content: In constructing a weighted k-nearest neighbor graph, the n × n weight matrix W has diagonal entries set to zero (Wii = 0 for i = 1, ..., n). The parameter k determines the number of nearest neighbors considered and is tied to the dimensionality d of the clusters; for clusters resembling d-dimensional surfaces, k should be at least d. A small k results in a sparse graph, limiting comparisons to nearby points, which is advantageous because Euclidean distance is a reasonable approximation only for points close together, such as points on the surface of a unit sphere where distance should ideally be measured along the surface. The parameter β controls the scale of the distances between points, serving a role similar to k but related to actual distance scale rather than neighborhood size.

relationships.target: k parameter depends on cluster dimensionality
small k leads to sparse graph limiting comparisons to nearby points
β parameter tied to scale of point distances

title: Graph Partitioning for Clustering
summary: Defines the clustering problem as partitioning n objects represented by a weighted graph into two disjoint groups using binary labels, where the graph weights represent similarity between objects.
content: The clustering problem is formally defined as partitioning n objects into two groups (binary partition). Objects are represented by a weighted graph with symmetric positive weights Wij = Wji ≥ 0, where Wij = 0 if no edge exists between nodes i and j, and Wii = 0. The goal is to partition the nodes into two disjoint groups C+ and C− such that C+ ∪ C− = {1, ..., n}. This partition corresponds to labeling nodes with binary labels yi ∈ {−1, 1}, where yi = 1 if node i ∈ C+. Thus, clusters can be specified either by the sets (C+, C−) or by the binary labeling vector y of length n.

title: Graph Cut and Normalized Cut Criteria for Binary Clustering
summary: This node describes the objective functions used for binary clustering in graph-based methods, including the cut value and the normalized cut criterion, highlighting their definitions, properties, and limitations.
content: In graph-based binary clustering, each clustering corresponds to a cut in the graph. The weight of the cut, denoted as s(C+, C−), is defined as the sum of the weights Wij of edges connecting nodes in different clusters C+ and C−. Formally, s(C+, C−) = Σ_{i∈C+, j∈C−} Wij = Σ_{i,j} Wij (y_i - y_j)^2 / 4, where (y_i - y_j)^2 equals 4 if nodes i and j have different labels and zero otherwise. The cut value is zero if all nodes share the same label. Minimizing this cut value under the constraint that both labels are present leads to the minimum cut criterion, which can be efficiently computed. However, this approach tends to isolate outliers as clusters and is not effective for balanced clustering. To address this, the normalized cut criterion (Shi and Malik 2000) is introduced, defined as Norm-cut(C+, C−) = s(C+, C−)/[s(C+, C+) + s(C+, C−)] + s(C+, C−)/[s(C−, C−) + s(C+, C−)], which aims to find more balanced clusters by normalizing the cut value with respect to the total connection weights within each cluster plus the cut.

title: Normalized Cut Criterion and Spectral Clustering Eigenvalue Relaxation
summary: The normalized cut criterion measures the quality of a graph partition by the ratio of the cut weight to the total weight of nodes in each cluster, promoting balanced partitions and preventing outliers from forming single clusters. The optimization problem is an integer programming problem, which is computationally hard, but can be approximated by relaxing the binary labeling to real values and solving an eigenvalue problem, leading to spectral clustering.
content:
The normalized cut (Norm-cut) criterion for partitioning a graph into two clusters C+ and C− is defined as:

Norm-cut(C+, C−) = s(C+, C−)/[s(C+, C+) + s(C+, C−)] + s(C+, C−)/[s(C−, C−) + s(C+, C−)]

where s(C+, C+) = \sum_{i \in C+, j \in C+} W_{ij} is the sum of weights between nodes within cluster C+, and similarly for other terms. Each term represents the fraction of the total weight associated with the cluster that is cut, thus normalizing the cut weight. This normalization discourages partitions that isolate outliers, as an outlier connected by a single small weight edge would have a cut fraction of 1, the maximum possible, preventing it from forming a single cluster.

However, finding the exact solution to minimizing the normalized cut is an integer programming problem and is computationally intractable. To approximate the solution, the binary cluster labeling is relaxed to real values z_i \in \mathbb{R}, interpreting the sign of z_i as the cluster assignment. This relaxation transforms the problem into an eigenvalue problem, which can be solved efficiently, forming the basis of spectral clustering.

title: Graph Laplacian and its Properties
summary: The graph Laplacian matrix L = D - W is defined from a weighted graph with weight matrix W and diagonal degree matrix D, and is positive semi-definite with smallest eigenvalue zero corresponding to the constant eigenvector.
content: Given a weighted graph with weight matrix W, where W is symmetric, define the diagonal matrix D with elements D_ii = \sum_j W_ij. The graph Laplacian matrix is defined as L = D - W. The quadratic form J(z) = \sum_{i,j} W_{ij} (z_i - z_j)^2 can be rewritten as J(z) = z^T L z. The matrix L is guaranteed to be positive semi-definite, meaning all its eigenvalues are non-negative. The smallest eigenvalue of L is exactly zero and corresponds to the constant eigenvector z = 1.

relationships.target: Smallest eigenvalue of L is zero
Eigenvector corresponding to smallest eigenvalue is constant vector z=1

title: Relaxed Normalized Cut Optimization via Eigenvector Computation
summary: The normalized cut objective is relaxed to a continuous optimization problem involving real-valued vectors z, with constraints to balance cluster weights and normalize z to avoid trivial solutions. The relaxed problem reduces to finding the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of the generalized eigenvalue problem (D - W)z = λDz or equivalently (I - D^{-1}W)z = λz.
content:
The normalized cut objective balances the overall weight associated with nodes in two clusters, expressed as s(C+, C+) + s(C+, C−) ≈ s(C−, C−) + s(C+, C−). This balance condition in terms of labels is y^T D 1 = 0, which is relaxed to z^T D 1 = 0 for real-valued vector z. To avoid trivial solutions where z approaches zero, normalization is imposed as z^T D z = 1. This normalization weights changes at nodes strongly connected to others more heavily, ensuring isolated nodes act as followers. The resulting relaxed optimization problem is:

minimize z^T (D - W) z
subject to z^T D z = 1, z^T D 1 = 0

This problem can be solved using Lagrange multipliers, reducing to finding the eigenvector z_2 corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue λ in the generalized eigenvalue problem:

(D - W) z = λ D z

or equivalently:

(I - D^{-1} W) z = λ z

title: Eigenvector Equation for Graph Clustering
summary: The eigenvector equation (D − W)z = λDz and its equivalent form (I − D^{-1}W)z = λz describe the spectral clustering problem. The eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue λ=0 is the constant vector z=1, which does not satisfy the constraint z^T D 1 = 0. Therefore, the second smallest eigenvector is used for clustering, focusing on eigenvectors with small eigenvalues to minimize z^T (D − W) z.
content: The eigenvector equation for spectral clustering is given by (D − W)z = λDz or equivalently (I − D^{-1}W)z = λz. The eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue λ=0 is the constant vector z=1, which does not satisfy the constraint z^T D 1 = 0. Hence, the second smallest eigenvector is used to find clusters. Since the objective is to minimize z^T (D − W) z, only eigenvectors with small eigenvalues are relevant. Clusters are identified by labeling nodes according to these eigenvectors.

title: Spectral Clustering and Random Walk Interpretation
summary: Spectral clustering solution involves labeling nodes based on the sign of components of the second eigenvector, with an option to balance cluster sizes by sorting these components. The relaxed optimization problem approximates the normalized cut problem and can be interpreted via random walks on the weighted graph, where eigenvectors of (I−D−1W)z=λz correspond to those of D−1Wz=λ' z with λ' = 1−λ, and the constant eigenvector corresponds to eigenvalue 1 in the random walk matrix.
content: In spectral clustering, nodes are labeled by yˆi = sign(z2i), where z2 is the second largest eigenvector. To balance cluster sizes, components of z2 can be sorted ascendingly and nodes labeled negative accordingly. Figure 2 illustrates this solution and eigenvector values. The relaxed optimization problem approximates the normalized cut problem but its behavior can be justified via random walks on the weighted graph. The eigenvectors solving (I−D−1W)z=λz are the same as those solving D−1Wz=λ' z, with eigenvalues related by λ' = 1−λ. The constant eigenvector z=1 with λ=0 corresponds to λ'=1 and satisfies D−1Wz = z. Transition probabilities are defined as Pij = Wij / Dii, representing the random walk on the graph.

relationships.target: Eigenvalues λ and λ' satisfy λ' = 1−λ
Constant eigenvector z=1 corresponds to eigenvalue λ=0 and λ'=1 in random walk matrix

title: Random Walk as a Markov Chain on a Weighted Graph
summary: The transition probability matrix P = D^{-1}W defines a random walk on a weighted graph, where P_{ij} represents the probability of moving from node i to node j. This random walk corresponds to a homogeneous Markov chain with states as graph nodes and time-invariant transition probabilities.
content: Given a weighted graph with weight matrix W and degree matrix D, the transition probability matrix P is defined as P = D^{-1}W, where P_{ij} = W_{ij} / D_{ii}. Each row of P sums to 1, i.e., \sum_j P_{ij} = 1, allowing interpretation of P as a transition probability matrix for a random walk on the graph. Specifically, P_{ij} defines the probability of hopping from node i to node j in one step. If X(t) denotes the node occupied at time t, then the transition probability satisfies P(X(t+1) = j | X(t) = i) = P_{ij}. This random walk is a homogeneous Markov chain because the transition probabilities do not depend on time. The states of this Markov chain correspond to the nodes of the graph.

title: Communicating States, Irreducibility, and Ergodicity in Markov Chains
summary: This node explains the concepts of communicating states, irreducibility, and ergodicity in Markov chains, including the nature of transition diagrams and m-step transition probabilities.
content:
In a Markov chain, two states i and j are said to be communicating if it is possible to transition from i to j and from j to i with finite probability. A Markov chain is irreducible if all pairs of states are communicating. For example, a random walk defined on a graph with two disconnected components is not irreducible because nodes across the components do not communicate.

Transition diagrams specify all permissible one-step transitions i → j where P_ij > 0, typically represented as directed graphs. However, when the transition weights are symmetric, the transition diagram reduces to an undirected graph or a directed graph with edges in both directions. Despite symmetric weights, the transition probabilities P_ij are not symmetric due to node-specific normalization terms D_ii. The zero entries in the transition matrix P_ij, indicating prohibited transitions, are symmetric.

Ergodicity is an important property of some Markov chains. The m-step transition probabilities are defined as:

P(X(t+1) = j | X(t) = i) = P_ij
P(X(t+2) = j | X(t) = i) = Σ_k P_ik P_kj = [P^2]_ij
...
P(X(t+m) = j | X(t) = i) = [P^m]_ij
